nameStory: This jumping spider is named after Nicholas Marcellus Hentz, a pioneering 19th-century arachnologist who described many North American spiders. The genus name Phlegra comes from Greek mythology, referring to the ancient battlefield where giants fought the gods - perhaps a nod to these spiders' bold hunting behavior.
description: Phlegra hentzi is a small jumping spider with the characteristic large front eyes and compact, robust body typical of its family. These spiders are active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch food. They're relatively small, usually measuring just a few millimeters in body length, but what they lack in size they make up for in personality and hunting prowess.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a row across the face, with the middle pair being noticeably larger and giving an almost cartoon-like appearance

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rectangular cephalothorax (front section) that feels firm to the touch, with a slightly fuzzy texture from tiny hairs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops to look around, often turning to face you if you approach slowly

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to sit comfortably on a dime, with legs that don't extend much beyond the body when at rest

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No hunting web, but may leave tiny silk safety lines behind as it moves, like a miniature rock climber's rope

habitat: Look for Phlegra hentzi on sunny surfaces like rocks, wooden fences, and tree bark where they hunt for small insects. They prefer open areas with good visibility rather than dense vegetation. You might spot them on south-facing stone walls or wooden structures that warm up in the afternoon sun.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on rocks and wooden surfaces during mild afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults hunting actively throughout the day. This is the best time to observe their stalking behavior and courtship displays.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, but spiders become less active as temperatures drop. Egg sacs may be found tucked under bark or in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Generally inactive, with young spiders overwintering in protected locations like under loose bark or in rock cracks.

funFact: These tiny spiders have vision that's proportionally better than a hawk's - they can spot and track prey from distances up to 20 times their own body length, which would be like you clearly seeing a mouse from nearly 100 feet away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the eye arrangement is the giveaway - if you can see four eyes in a clear front row with the middle two being largest, you're looking at a jumping spider. Remember: 'Four in front, jumpers about!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'jumping' spiders, they don't actually jump to catch prey like grasshoppers do. Instead, they make controlled leaps as an escape mechanism or to move between hunting perches, always trailing a safety line of silk.
compareHints: Since Phlegra hentzi is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, compare it with other small jumping spiders in the Salticidae family. It tends to be more compact and rectangular than the more elongated wolf spiders, and lacks the distinctive white mustache markings of some Habronattus species.
